dmaic.intro: DMAIC is the core methodology of Six Sigma — a structured, data-driven approach for the sustainable improvement of existing processes. Its five phases Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve and Control lead you systematically from a vaguely perceived problem to a proven, permanently anchored solution.
dmaic.whyBody: Many improvement projects fail because they jump to a solution too early. DMAIC enforces discipline: first understand, then measure, then analyse — only then change. Decisions rest on data rather than opinions, and success is proven quantitatively at the end. That makes the methodology robust against gut-feel fixes and creates a transparent thread the whole project team can follow.
dmaic.defineBody: In the Define phase you clarify what the project is really about: which problem shall be solved, for whom, by when, and how will benefit and success be measured? Typical tools are the Project Charter with measurable goals (Goal Achievement Level, GAL), a coarse SIPOC to scope the process, a stakeholder analysis, and VOC/CTQ to translate customer voice into critical quality characteristics. The output is a tightly scoped project charter that everyone involved can agree on.
dmaic.measureBody: Before you improve, you need to know where you stand. The Measure phase delivers reliable data: a clean process description (process map), a trustworthy measurement method (MSA Type 1, Gage R&R) and baseline indicators for capability (Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk) and stability. Without a validated measurement system later improvements can neither be detected nor proven — which is why a sound measurement system is the central prerequisite for everything that follows.
dmaic.analyzeBody: Now you search systematically for the true root causes — not the symptoms. Ishikawa and 5-Why structure the thinking, correlation and hypothesis tests (t-test, ANOVA, Chi², regression) verify which suspected drivers are actually statistically significant. At the end of this phase you know the few critical X that really drive the Y of your process.
dmaic.improveBody: With the root-cause knowledge from Analyze you develop solutions and test them — ideally via a Design of Experiments (DOE) that varies multiple factors systematically at once. This reveals the best factor combination with evidence, quantifies interactions and avoids expensive one-factor-at-a-time trials. Pilot runs confirm the effect under real conditions before the change goes into the production process.
dmaic.controlBody: The best improvement evaporates without control. In Control you introduce control charts (SPC), update work instructions, assign responsibilities and define a reaction plan for deviations. At the end of this phase the project's success is verified against the goals agreed in Define, recorded in a Lessons-Learned document and formally handed over to the process owner.
dmaic.whenTitle: When is DMAIC the right tool?
dmaic.whenBody: DMAIC is particularly suited to existing processes with measurable performance whose causes for deviation are unclear. For new designs, DMADV (Design for Six Sigma) is more appropriate, and for quick wins Kaizen or PDCA. A DMAIC project is worth it when the problem is economically significant, the causes are unclear, and data is fundamentally available (or obtainable).
dmaic.pitfall1: Jumping to a solution too early — without an understood root cause it stays symptom fighting, and the problem comes back.
dmaic.pitfall2: Skipping the measurement system. If the measurement itself adds 30 % variation, every baseline number is unreliable.
dmaic.pitfall3: Scoping too broadly. A tightly bounded project scope beats an ambitious "fix everything" project every time.
dmaic.pitfall4: Neglecting the Control phase. Without control mechanisms and clear ownership the process drifts back within a few months.
dmaic.appBody: The header shows six phase tiles (Data, D, M, A, I, C). Each phase is a container into which you add the matching modules (Project Charter, SIPOC, MSA, Process Capability, Hypothesis Tests, DOE, Control Charts, Lessons Learned …) via the hamburger menu (☰) on each tile. That way your project grows step by step along the methodology — and can be exported to JSON, archived and re-imported at any time.

dmadv.intro: DMADV stands for Define · Measure · Analyze · Design · Verify and is the Design-for-Six-Sigma variant of the improvement cycle. Instead of fixing an existing process, DMADV helps you design a new process or product from scratch so it meets the required quality characteristics reliably and reproducibly.
dmadv.whyBody: DMAIC works beautifully when a process is already running and just needs to be optimised. For greenfield development — a new product, a new service line, a new manufacturing step — the baseline data DMAIC relies on is missing. DMADV replaces "improving" with systematic "designing": first the customer needs and critical-to-quality characteristics are captured, then the design is selected from data-driven alternatives, and finally it is verified that the design meets the spec under realistic conditions.
dmadv.defineTitle: Define — Sharpen the charter and customer requirements
dmadv.defineBody: As in DMAIC, DMADV starts with a clear project charter: what is to be built, for whom, with what business benefit, by when? But the customer focus is stronger — Voice of the Customer (VOC), stakeholder analysis and an initial requirements brief. By the end of the phase you have a charter that pins down development scope and success criteria from both customer and business perspectives.
dmadv.measureBody: This phase translates the customer needs from Define into measurable critical-to-quality characteristics (CTQs). Which properties must the finished product or new process exhibit? Which tolerances are acceptable, which minimum performance is non-negotiable? If reference data from similar processes is available, measurement systems are evaluated (MSA) and baseline metrics captured — they later serve as the comparison basis for the Verify phase.
dmadv.analyzeBody: DMADV-Analyze differs significantly from DMAIC-Analyze: instead of hunting for root causes, several design concepts are systematically compared. Pugh matrices, concept scoring, concept-level FMEA, statistical predictions and (where appropriate) simulations help you select the most promising concept. Hypothesis tests and correlations can already be used here to validate assumptions about how the future system will behave.
dmadv.designTitle: Design — Work the chosen concept out in detail
dmadv.designBody: The concept selected in Analyze is fleshed out into a concrete, technically detailed design. Factor designs (DOE) help identify critical control parameters and their optimal settings, regression builds prediction models for the key metrics, detailed-level FMEA surfaces remaining risks. Pilot builds or prototypes deliver the first hard data with which the design is iteratively optimised before the final verification.
dmadv.verifyTitle: Verify — Confirm the design in practice
dmadv.verifyBody: Verify is the DMADV equivalent of DMAIC-Control: the finished design is tested under real or near-production conditions. Process capability analyses (Cp, Cpk), control charts and hypothesis tests check whether the CTQs agreed in Define are actually met. Once the spec is reached, the design moves into series production / steady-state operation together with the lessons-learned, work instructions and reaction plan.
dmadv.whenTitle: When is DMADV the right tool?
dmadv.whenBody: DMADV fits when something new is to be created: a new product, a new service, a new manufacturing process or a fundamentally re-thought variant of an existing process. Even when an existing process has been improved to the point where further DMAIC iterations yield diminishing returns, DMADV can be the next logical step to redesign the process from the ground up. For correcting a running process, however, DMAIC remains the more efficient choice.
dmadv.pitfall1: Filling Define with solution descriptions instead of requirements — the design gets unconsciously narrowed to a predetermined solution before alternatives have even been examined.
dmadv.pitfall2: Skipping VOC and CTQs or formulating them only qualitatively. Without measurable target values, Verify lacks the yardstick against which the design can be judged.
dmadv.pitfall3: Jumping into detailed design too early, before Analyze has fairly compared multiple concepts — you save weeks now and pay months later.
dmadv.pitfall4: Treating Verify as a mere formality. If you don't test the design under realistic conditions, you hand risks over to operations that come back later as "unexplained" quality problems.
dmadv.appBody: When you create a project with the "DMADV" cycle, the header shows seven tiles (Data, D, M, A, D, V, More). Modules like SIPOC, FMEA, MSA or Hypothesis Tests are mapped to the matching phases automatically; DOE and regression live in the Design phase, control charts and lessons-learned in Verify. Tools without a fixed DMADV mapping appear in the right "More" tile and can be drag-and-dropped into a phase — full access to the entire toolkit is preserved.

eightd.intro: The 8D cycle (Eight Disciplines) is a structured problem-solving process for reactive defect resolution — typically triggered by a customer complaint, a recurring production defect or a safety incident. Across eight disciplines (nine when counting D0) it walks the team from immediate containment through root-cause analysis to durable prevention and finally formal recognition of the team.
eightd.whyBody: When a problem turns acute — complaint, line stop, recall — there isn't time for a multi-month DMAIC project. A quick fix alone won't do either: customers, auditors and your own quality system demand evidence that the problem is understood, durably fixed and prevented going forward. 8D delivers exactly that framework — short enough for real-world response times, thorough enough for a genuine root-cause investigation, and documented enough for a formal 8D report to the customer.
eightd.prepareBody: Before the team is formed, D0 settles the entry criteria: is this an 8D case (recurring defect, safety issue, customer complaint) or a routine deviation? Emergency Response Actions to contain immediate harm are documented here. D0 ends with a decision on whether 8D is the right process at all — and which initial safeguards take effect immediately.
eightd.teamBody: 8D is teamwork: you need representatives of every function that can understand, contain or durably resolve the problem — production, quality, engineering, supplier, service. Define champion, team leader, core team and extended team; clarify responsibilities (RACI); and make sure the team has the necessary decision authority and time.
eightd.problemBody: A precisely described problem is half solved. The standard structure is "Is / Is Not" (what occurs, what doesn't?) along the 5W2H questions (What, Where, When, Who, Why, How, How much). SIPOC, process maps and Voice-of-the-Customer collections help capture the problem objectively and verifiably — without premature blame and without hypotheses about the cause.
eightd.containmentBody: D3 protects the customer before the root cause is known. Typical containment actions: 100% inspection, sorting, quarantine of affected lots, replacement at the customer, additional incoming inspection. Crucially, containment is explicitly temporary and its effectiveness is monitored. It never replaces the permanent solution — it merely buys time for it.
eightd.rootcauseBody: D4 hunts the true causes — separately for the occurrence cause (why did the defect arise?), the escape cause (why wasn't it caught?) and the systemic cause (which gap in the management system allowed this?). 5-Why, Ishikawa, hypothesis tests and correlations validate suspicions rigorously. By the end of D4, causes are statistically or physically proven, not just plausible.
eightd.correctiveBody: With the cause known, the team plans Permanent Corrective Actions and picks the most effective option among alternatives. Evaluation criteria: effectiveness against the cause, freedom from risk (FMEA), effort, transferability to similar processes. Before rollout the effectiveness is verified — ideally via a designed experiment (DOE), a simulation or a limited pilot.
eightd.implementationBody: D6 rolls out the planned actions across the full scope and validates their effect in live operation. Control charts and capability analyses demonstrate that the problem no longer occurs. Once effectiveness is confirmed, the D3 containment actions are deliberately retired — the process now runs stably without crutches.
eightd.preventBody: D7 lifts the findings to the system level: which standards, specifications, work instructions, FMEAs, training plans and inspection routines must be updated so this problem cannot reappear anywhere — not in similar products or processes either? This is where the real learning leverage of 8D lies: a single defect becomes a permanent improvement to the management system.
eightd.recognizeBody: The closing step must never be skipped: make the success visible, formally discharge the team, document and communicate the lessons learned. Without this recognition, 8D processes lose internal acceptance — teams contribute less at the next incident if last time their effort vanished without comment. D8 is therefore not bureaucratic residue, but a central element of culture-building.
eightd.whenBody: 8D fits when a concrete defect has already occurred and needs reactive resolution — customer complaint, recurring production defect, audit finding, safety incident. Characteristic features: short time horizon (days to a few weeks), clear accountability to a recipient (customer, regulator), and the obligation to deliver solid documentation in the form of an 8D report. For proactive improvements without an acute trigger DMAIC remains the better choice; for greenfield development DMADV.
eightd.pitfall1: Treating D3 as the final solution. Sorting and 100% inspection are containment actions, not corrective actions — stopping here hides rather than solves the real problem.
eightd.pitfall2: Ending root-cause analysis at the first plausible explanation. Real 5-Why chains push at least to the systemic cause ("why does our process even allow this defect?") — anything shorter remains symptom treatment.
eightd.pitfall3: Forgetting D7. Implementing corrective actions only on the affected product without updating similar products / processes / FMEAs / work instructions guarantees that the same defect reappears six months later on a sister line.
eightd.pitfall4: Treating D8 as a chore. No thank-you, no communication of lessons learned, no visible value for the team — and at the next 8D call the most important people quietly opt out.
eightd.appBody: When you create a project with the "8D" cycle, the header shows eleven tiles (Data, D0…D8, More). Project Charter, SIPOC and VOC live in D2, Five-Why and Ishikawa in D4, DOE and Regression in D5, control charts in D6, FMEA in D7 and Lessons Learned in D8. Prepare (D0) and Containment (D3) currently lack dedicated modules — until those exist you can use the Todo list in D1/D3 to document entry checks and containment actions.

minitab.intro: Welcome to Qprovement! This page helps Minitab users get started. A lot will feel familiar — below we show where to find your usual features and how things are organised differently here.
minitab.conceptsIntro: Minitab works with a project that contains multiple worksheets. Qprovement follows a similar model but additionally organises work along the DMAIC phases (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control).
minitab.mappingIntro: The table below maps typical Minitab menu entries to their Qprovement equivalent.
minitab.row1c: Worksheets live in the central Data area and are not bound to any DMAIC phase — every analysis module can access every worksheet.
minitab.row2a: Stat → Basic Statistics → Display Descriptive Statistics
minitab.row2c: Results appear in the output panel next to the input.
minitab.row3c: Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk are computed automatically.
minitab.row4c: X̄-R, I-MR, p, np, c, u — all the Minitab standard charts are available.
minitab.row5b: Charts live inside the respective analysis modules
minitab.row5c: No separate Graph menu — charts are produced in context.
minitab.row6c: ANOVA is part of the Hypothesis Test module in the Analyze phase. Regression lives in the Improve phase, where it is typically used for model building.
minitab.row7c: Factorial designs, response surface and Plackett-Burman included.
minitab.row8c: Type-1 and Type-2 studies as standalone modules.
minitab.workflowIntro: While in Minitab you usually open a worksheet and launch analyses from the Stat menu, Qprovement is project-oriented:
minitab.workflow1: Create a new project at the top left (or open an existing one).
minitab.workflow2: Pick the DMAIC phase you want to work in (D, M, A, I, C).
minitab.workflow3: Add modules to that phase via the hamburger menu (☰) on the phase tile — each module is a tool (worksheet, chart, test, charter, …).
minitab.workflow4: Modules open as tabs in the workspace — similar to multiple worksheets in Minitab, but grouped by phase.
minitab.workflow5: Results are saved into the project automatically (local browser storage). Use the Export/Import buttons at the top to save projects as JSON.
minitab.dataBody: The worksheet module behaves like a Minitab worksheet: named columns, keyboard cell editing, copy/paste between Excel and the worksheet. CSV and XLSX import/export are available inside the module. Unlike Minitab, analysis modules pick their data source explicitly via a column picker — so you can always tell which data was used.
minitab.tip1: Session window: Qprovement has no classic session window. Each analysis appears in the output area of its module and stays there while the module is open.
minitab.tip2: Everything stays local: your projects and data are stored only in the browser (localStorage/IndexedDB) — there is no server and no cloud. That keeps them private, but it also means they can be lost if the browser cache is cleared, the profile is reset, or you switch to a different machine. Save your projects regularly via the Export button in the top header as a JSON file — you can restore them at any time through "Import".
minitab.tip3: Module help: as soon as a module is active, a question-mark icon appears in the top-right header — directly to the left of this training icon. Clicking it opens a module-specific guide with methodology, examples and common pitfalls. The icon is only visible when the active module has help content registered.
minitab.tip4: Validation: every statistical algorithm is validated against reference values (Minitab, R, NIST). The "Developing" area contains the Algorithm Lab with source code, formulas and test cases.

jmp.intro: Welcome to Qprovement! Coming from JMP, a lot will feel familiar — interactive charts, column roles, a central data-table model. This section shows where to find your usual analyses and what is deliberately organised differently here.
jmp.conceptsIntro: JMP is built around a data table and launches analyses from the Analyze and Graph menus. Qprovement also has central worksheets, but groups its tools along the DMAIC phases (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control) rather than through a global analyse menu.
jmp.mappingIntro: The table below maps typical JMP menu entries to their Qprovement equivalent.
jmp.row1c: Worksheets live in the central Data area and are not bound to any DMAIC phase. Roles are not assigned globally but inside each analysis module.
jmp.row2c: The Distribution platform is split across several dedicated modules.
jmp.row3c: Which module applies depends — as in JMP — on the data types (continuous/categorical). ANOVA is part of the Hypothesis Test module.
jmp.row4a: Analyze → Quality and Process → Process Capability
jmp.row4c: Cp, Cpk, Pp, Ppk including a normality check.
jmp.row5a: Analyze → Quality and Process → Control Chart Builder
jmp.row5c: X̄-R, I-MR, p, np, c, u — with rule violations highlighted.
jmp.row6a: Analyze → Quality and Process → Measurement Systems Analysis
jmp.row6c: Type-1 and Type-2 studies as standalone modules.
jmp.row7c: Factorial designs, response surface and screening designs included.
jmp.row8b: Charts live inside the respective analysis modules
jmp.row8c: There is no free-form Graph Builder — charts are produced in the context of the module that analyses them.
jmp.workflowIntro: In JMP you open a data table and launch analyses from the menu. Qprovement is more project- and phase-oriented:
jmp.workflow1: Create a new project at the top left (or open an existing one).
jmp.workflow2: Pick the DMAIC phase you want to work in (D, M, A, I, C).
jmp.workflow3: Add modules to that phase via the hamburger menu (☰) on the phase tile — each module is a tool (worksheet, chart, test, charter, …).
jmp.workflow4: Analysis modules pick their data explicitly via a column picker from a worksheet — this is our counterpart to JMP's role assignment (X, Y, By, Freq, …).
jmp.workflow5: Results are saved into the project automatically (local browser storage). Use the Export/Import buttons at the top to save projects as JSON.
jmp.dataBody: The worksheet module plays the role of the JMP data table: named columns with types, keyboard cell editing, copy/paste from Excel. CSV and XLSX import/export are available inside the module. Column roles (X, Y, By, …) are not set on the worksheet itself but when you open an analysis module, via the column picker — so the same worksheet remains freely reusable across multiple analyses.
jmp.tip1: Interactive charts: charts in Qprovement support zoom, pan and tooltips, but they are not dynamically linked the way JMP "row state" connects views. Filtered views are produced by explicit selection inside the analysis module.
jmp.tip2: Everything stays local: your projects and data are stored only in the browser (localStorage/IndexedDB) — there is no server and no cloud. That keeps them private, but it also means they can be lost if the browser cache is cleared, the profile is reset, or you switch to a different machine. Save your projects regularly via the Export button in the top header as a JSON file — you can restore them at any time through "Import".
jmp.tip3: Module help: as soon as a module is active, a question-mark icon appears in the top-right header — directly to the left of this training icon. Clicking it opens a module-specific guide with methodology, examples and common pitfalls. The icon is only visible when the active module has help content registered.
jmp.tip4: JSL & scripting: Qprovement has no scripting language like JSL (yet). Reproducibility is achieved through the JSON export of the entire project — including every module state and worksheet.

triz.intro: TRIZ (Theory of Inventive Problem Solving, Russian "Teoriya Resheniya Izobretatelskikh Zadach") is a systematic innovation methodology that the Soviet engineer Genrich Altshuller developed from 1946 onwards by analysing hundreds of thousands of patents. While DMAIC improves existing processes, TRIZ helps resolve technical contradictions — situations where improving one property has so far inevitably worsened another.
triz.whyBody: Classical innovation tools such as brainstorming or trial-and-error rely on quantity — many ideas in the hope that one of them is good. TRIZ relies on pattern recognition instead: Altshuller showed that most inventive solutions stem from roughly 40 recurring principles, regardless of the field. Once you formulate a contradiction cleanly, you can look up historically proven solution paths instead of reinventing the wheel every time. Inventing turns from a flash of inspiration into a reproducible procedure.
triz.contradictionBody: A technical contradiction exists when improving one parameter degrades another (example: a car should become safer — i.e. heavier — but at the same time more fuel-efficient — i.e. lighter). A physical contradiction demands two opposite properties of the same element (hot and cold, hard and soft, present and absent). Inventive solutions resolve the contradiction rather than smoothing it over with a compromise.
triz.idealityBody: The Ideal Final Result (IFR) is a thought experiment: what if the desired function were delivered without a system, without cost and without harmful side-effects? TRIZ holds that technical systems evolve towards higher ideality — more benefit per cost, fewer parts, fewer harmful effects. The IFR sharpens the goal and prevents you from getting trapped inside the existing solution.
triz.evolutionBody: Altshuller identified eight laws by which technical systems evolve (e.g. increasing completeness, transition to the micro-level, dynamisation, self-adaptation). Rating your system's maturity against these laws reveals which evolutionary leaps are likely next — and which competing solutions will probably appear in the medium term.
triz.tool40Body: A library of 40 generic solution patterns (e.g. "Segmentation", "Prior action", "The other way round", "Phase transition"). Every principle is phrased abstractly and transfers across industries — from refrigerators to software architecture.
triz.toolMatrixBody: A 39×39 matrix that lists typical "improving" against "worsening" parameters. Each cell points to the statistically most frequent principles for that contradiction. The matrix shrinks the search space from "which of the 40 ideas applies?" down to "which 3–4 principles have proven useful for this exact constellation in the patent record?".
triz.tool9WindowsBody: A 3×3 grid that views the system on two axes simultaneously: hierarchy (subsystem · system · supersystem) and time (past · present · future). The tool breaks the tunnel-vision by deliberately forcing you into the neighbouring cell — opening up solution spaces that purely present-state thinking never reaches.
triz.toolArizTitle: ARIZ — Algorithm for Inventive Problem Solving
triz.toolArizBody: The heavyweight in the TRIZ toolbox: a nine-step algorithm that turns a vaguely formulated problem step-by-step into a physical contradiction and finally into its resolution. ARIZ is typically reserved for situations where the 40 principles and the contradiction matrix do not lead directly to a solution.
triz.whenTitle: When is TRIZ the right tool?
triz.whenBody: TRIZ shines whenever classical brainstorming or trial-and-error stall — typically with hard technical contradictions, in innovation and engineering work, or when an existing system has hit the limits of its architecture. For purely statistical process optimisation (reduce variation, raise Cpk), DMAIC remains the superior tool. TRIZ and DMAIC are not mutually exclusive: in the Improve phase of a DMAIC project, TRIZ can help when the identified root causes create what looks like an unavoidable trade-off.
triz.pitfall1: Giving up on the contradiction too early. If you don't formulate the trade-off cleanly, you fall back on a compromise ("a little more safety against a little more weight") and waste the chance for an inventive solution.
triz.pitfall2: Taking the 40 principles literally. They are abstract solution patterns, not finished blueprints — translating them onto your specific problem still requires thinking.
triz.pitfall3: Using TRIZ as a brainstorming add-on. Without a clean formulation of function, ideality and contradiction, TRIZ collapses into a list of buzzwords and loses its systematic edge.
triz.pitfall4: Watering down the Ideal Final Result during the real design. The strength of the IFR is precisely that it does not have to be reachable — it only points the direction. Making it "realistic" too early destroys exactly that orientation.
triz.appBody: Qprovement contains two TRIZ tools in the Improve phase: the "9 Windows" module for system analysis across hierarchy and time, and the "Contradiction Matrix" module with the 39 parameters and 40 principles after Altshuller. Both modules persist their state inside the project and can be JSON-exported and re-imported like any other module. You reach them via the hamburger menu (☰) on the Improve tile, or by drag-and-dropping them from the "More" tile into another phase if you want to use TRIZ already in the Define or Analyze step.

modules.intro: This overview shows which modules are preconfigured for each phase of a cycle. Modules without a phase mapping in the active cycle land in the "More" tile (⋯) and can be drag-and-dropped from there into any phase.
modules.dataIntro: These modules belong to the global data area and are available in every cycle. They are grouped by task.
modules.cyclesIntro: For each cycle, the table lists the phases and the modules preconfigured for them. Modules that may also be used in additional allowed phases are noted in parentheses as "also in: …".
modules.extrasIntro: These modules have no preconfigured phase mapping in this cycle and appear in the "More" tile.

dashboard.title: Dashboard
dashboard.noHistory: No GAL entries recorded yet. Set a value with the pencil on a phase tile or enter it under “Edit data”.
dashboard.vocEmpty: No VoC module created or no VoC statements recorded.
dashboard.spcEmpty: No control chart configured (no column selected).
dashboard.spcNoData: Too few data points for a control chart.
dashboard.capabilityEmpty: No capability analysis configured (no column selected).
dashboard.capabilityNoData: No analysable data (at least two values and one specification limit needed).
dashboard.attrSpcEmpty: No attribute control chart configured (no defects column selected).
dashboard.attrSpcNoData: Too few valid points for a control chart.

datagrid.scanAllMatch: All values share the same type
datagrid.roleContinuousTooltip: Numeric values on a continuous scale (e.g. length, weight, temperature). Used for mean, standard deviation, regression, capability analysis.
datagrid.roleCategoricalTooltip: Discrete groups without order (e.g. Machine A/B/C, Shift Day/Night). Used for frequencies, Pareto, chi-square tests, group comparisons.
datagrid.roleOrdinalTooltip: Ordered categories with ranking but no uniform spacing (e.g. small/medium/large, grades 1–6). Used for rank-based tests.
datagrid.roleDateTooltip: Date or time for time series, trend charts, and control charts with a time axis.
datagrid.roleIdentifierTooltip: Unique identifier of a record (e.g. sample ID, serial number, batch). Used as the row label in result tables and drill-downs (e.g. flagged outliers) so a finding can be traced back to the physical sample. Excluded from statistical calculations.
datagrid.roleFreeTextTooltip: Unstructured text such as notes or comments. Excluded from calculations.

SeriesStats.name: Name of the series, as in the Series column and the legend: the column name, or the group value when grouped.
SeriesStats.stats: The figures of this series, each described individually. Empty for a series without values; the table then shows dashes.
SeriesStats.ci: The confidence intervals of this series at the chosen level, for mean, spread and variance. The table shows them after the value, as lower and upper bound. Empty if the series has fewer than two values or no spread. The table rounds the bounds to four decimals, magnitudes below 0.001 or from 10⁶ up to four significant digits.

Stats.n: Number of values in the series (N); the table shows it as a whole number.
Stats.mean: Mean x̄ = Σx / n, the sum of all values divided by their count. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.stddev: Standard deviation s = √(Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)), the sample spread with denominator n − 1 (column StdDev). The table rounds to four decimals. With only one value it is undefined: the table shows a dash, and in the agent result the value is empty.
Stats.variance: Variance s² = Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1), the square of the standard deviation, with denominator n − 1. The table rounds to four decimals. With only one value it is undefined: the table shows a dash, and in the agent result the value is empty.
Stats.seMean: Standard error of the mean, s / √n. The table does not show it; it is what sets the width of the confidence interval for the mean. With only one value it is undefined; in the agent result the value is empty.
Stats.median: Median: the middle of the values sorted ascending, for an even count the mean of the two middle ones. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.min: Smallest value of the series. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.max: Largest value of the series. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.range: Range = largest minus smallest value. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.q1: First quartile: the limit below which a quarter of the sorted values lie, with linear interpolation between neighbouring values. The table does not show it.
Stats.q3: Third quartile: the limit below which three quarters of the sorted values lie, with linear interpolation between neighbouring values. The table does not show it.
Stats.skewness: Skewness g₁ = m₃ / m₂^1.5 with the central moments m₂ = Σ(x − x̄)² / n and m₃ = Σ(x − x̄)³ / n (denominator n, not corrected). Positive: the long tail is on the right, negative: on the left; 0 for symmetric values and for a series without spread. The table rounds to four decimals.
Stats.kurtosis: Kurtosis as excess: m₄ / m₂² − 3 with m₂ = Σ(x − x̄)² / n and m₄ = Σ(x − x̄)⁴ / n (denominator n, not corrected). 0 matches the normal distribution, positive means more peaked with heavy tails, negative flatter; 0 for a series without spread. The table rounds to four decimals.

StatsCi.mean: Confidence interval for the mean: x̄ ± t · s / √n with the t quantile at n − 1 degrees of freedom. Missing for fewer than two values or without spread.
StatsCi.variance: Confidence interval for the variance: from (n − 1)·s² / χ²(upper) to (n − 1)·s² / χ²(lower), with the χ² quantiles at n − 1 degrees of freedom. Missing for fewer than two values, without spread, or if a χ² quantile cannot be computed.
StatsCi.stddev: Confidence interval for the standard deviation: the square roots of the variance interval's bounds. Missing for fewer than two values, without spread, or if a χ² quantile cannot be computed.

read.help: Returns the full read state of this instance. Without parameters bulk data stays out and appears as a scope descriptor, so it can be requested deliberately instead of transferring thousands of rows.

params.options: Optional selection: "fields" names the bulk fields to be delivered in full; "rows" trims each of them to the range from "from" to "to".

worksheet.name: Data Collection
worksheet.description: Spreadsheet for data entry and management
worksheet.whenToUse: The shared data substrate: measurements land here before an analysing tool reads them through a column reference. Almost every analysis starts with a data collection.

read.help: Returns the sheet list, the active sheet and the column headers; the rows come only on request via options.fields = ['rows'].

params.options: Optional: fields: ['rows'] returns the rows, rows: { from, to } trims them.

importCsv.help: Replaces the active sheet's content with CSV data. Delimiter and header row are detected; the step can be reverted with undo.

params.csvText: The full CSV or TSV text, header row included if present.

setCells.help: Writes a block of values into one column, downwards from a row. Type detection, locks and undo as with cell entry. Values only: a formula such as =C1*2 is written as text, not evaluated — formulas stay with the formula editor in the UI. A plain value written into a formula cell OVERWRITES the formula — read().formulas says which cells are computed; undo restores value and formula.

params.columnId: The id of the target column, as read().columns[].id names it.
params.startRow: Zero-based index of the first row.
params.values: The values, one per row; formula text is not evaluated.

addColumn.help: Appends an empty column to the active sheet.

addRows.help: Appends empty rows to the active sheet.

params.count: Number of rows; ten without an argument, like the toolbar button.

undo.help: Reverts the last change to the sheet.

addSheet.help: Creates a new sheet and makes it active. The agent receives its id.

switchSheet.help: Switches to this sheet; the table and everything an agent reads afterwards refer to it. Double-click renames it.

params.id: The id of the sheet, as read().sheets[].id names it.
The id of the sheet.
params.name: The new name; empty or whitespace only is an invalid argument and therefore an error.

stakeholder-analysis.name: Stakeholder Analysis
stakeholder-analysis.description: Identify, assess, and plan communication with project stakeholders
stakeholder-analysis.noStakeholdersHint: Add your first stakeholder to start the analysis.
stakeholder-analysis.notesPlaceholder: What does this stakeholder expect? What concerns do they have?
stakeholder-analysis.whenToUse: When the stakeholders of a project need recording and placing by power and interest so that communication can follow that order; not for assigning responsibility to activities, which is what the RACI matrix is for.

addStakeholder.help: Adds a stakeholder and returns their id.

params.data: An object with name (required) and optionally role, power and interest (each a whole number from 1 to 5; default 3), support (supporter, neutral or critic; default neutral), category (intern, extern, kunde, lieferant or behoerde; default intern) and notes. A value outside the named sets is an error, as is a missing object and an object that names no name; an empty name adds nothing and returns null — that is a refusal, not an error.

updateStakeholder.help: Changes the named fields of a stakeholder; all others stay as they are.

params.id: The id of the stakeholder as read() lists it under stakeholders. An unknown id is an error.
params.data: An object holding exactly the fields that should change — name, role, power, interest, support, category or notes. Whatever is not in it stays unchanged. A value outside the named sets is an error, as is an object that names none of these fields; an empty name passed in changes nothing and returns false.

params.id: The id of the stakeholder as read() lists it under stakeholders. An unknown id is an error.

quadrants.help: The priority quadrant of each stakeholder, as a pair of id and quadrant, in the order of stakeholders; derived from power and interest.

stakeholders.help: The stakeholders in the order they were added, each entry described individually under keys. The priority quadrant follows from power and interest and is not stored; the quadrant of each entry is listed under quadrants. From a project import support and category may also carry a value other than the ones the actions accept.

StakeholderEntry.id: The identifier of the stakeholder; the app assigns it when the stakeholder is created. Use it to address the stakeholder when changing or removing.
StakeholderEntry.name: The name of the stakeholder, up to 100 characters. It is the only required entry.
StakeholderEntry.role: The role or organization of the stakeholder, up to 200 characters, for example department head or supplier.
StakeholderEntry.power: The stakeholder's power over the project, an integer from 1 (low) to 5 (high); 3 when not given. Together with interest it decides the quadrant of the power-interest matrix: 4 and above counts as high.
StakeholderEntry.interest: The stakeholder's interest in the project, an integer from 1 (low) to 5 (high); 3 when not given. Together with power it decides the quadrant of the power-interest matrix: 4 and above counts as high; high on both gives Manage Closely, only power high Keep Satisfied, only interest high Keep Informed, otherwise Monitor.
StakeholderEntry.support: The stakeholder's attitude to the project: supporter (Supporter), neutral (Neutral, the default) or critic (Critic). A critic with high power and high interest triggers the warning about critics among the key stakeholders. A value from an import or an older project may differ; the module takes it over as it is; whoever opens the entry in the form and saves it resets it to Neutral. In the matrix it is coloured like a critic, the table shows it without translation; it does not count toward the warning.
StakeholderEntry.category: The category of the stakeholder: intern (Internal, the default), extern (External), kunde (Customer), lieferant (Supplier) or behoerde (Authority). A value from an import or an older project may differ; the module takes it over as it is and shows it without translation; whoever opens the entry in the form and saves it resets it to Internal.
StakeholderEntry.notes: The stakeholder's expectations and concerns as free text, up to 500 characters.

AgentRead.quadrants: The priority quadrant of each stakeholder, as a pair of id and quadrant. It follows from power and interest (a value of 4 or more counts as high) and is not stored: manage-closely (Manage Closely) for high power and high interest, keep-satisfied (Keep Satisfied) for high power and low interest, keep-informed (Keep Informed) for low power and high interest, monitor (Monitor) for both low. The Quadrant column of the overview shows it.

stakeholder-analysis.criticWarningText: {names} — managing closely means: address their concerns and involve them before they block the project.

voc-ctx-tree.name: VoC → CTx Tree
voc-ctx-tree.description: Translate Voice of Customer into measurable CTx requirements
voc-ctx-tree.noVocs: No VoC statements yet. Start with the button above.
voc-ctx-tree.emptyTree: Select or create a VoC statement to build the CTx tree.
voc-ctx-tree.vocPlaceholder: e.g. I don't want to wait more than 2 days for my delivery.
voc-ctx-tree.reqPlaceholder: e.g. Delivery time ≤ 48h in 95% of cases
voc-ctx-tree.colorVocTip: Voice of Customer – Original customer statement about expectations, needs, or pain points
voc-ctx-tree.colorCtqTip: Critical to Quality – Quality characteristic that is decisive for the customer
voc-ctx-tree.colorCtdTip: Critical to Delivery – Delivery characteristic that is decisive for the customer
voc-ctx-tree.colorCtcTip: Critical to Cost – Cost characteristic that is decisive for the customer
voc-ctx-tree.whenToUse: When customer statements should be translated into a chain of requirements — the voice of the customer, the need behind it, the measurable driver (CTQ, CTD, CTC) and the testable requirement with a target value and a measure; not for collecting or rating customer statements themselves, that is what the survey and Kano tools are for.

addVoc.help: Adds a voice-of-customer statement and selects it.

params.text: The wording of the statement. Empty wording adds nothing and returns null; a missing argument is an error.
params.source: Where the statement came from, e.g. a survey, an interview or a complaint. Empty means no source; anything but text is an error.

updateVoc.help: Changes the wording and source of a voice-of-customer statement.

params.vocId: The id of the statement as read() lists it under vocs. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new wording. Empty wording changes nothing and returns false; a missing argument is an error.
params.source: The new source. An empty string clears it; a missing argument is an error.

removeVoc.help: Removes a voice-of-customer statement with its whole tree. If it was selected, the first remaining one takes over.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.

setActiveVoc.help: Selects the voice-of-customer statement whose tree is shown. In the list below, one click on a card is enough; with no selection the area stays empty.

params.vocId: The id of the statement, or null for no selection. Any other value is an error.

addNeed.help: Adds a need under a voice-of-customer statement.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The wording of the need. Empty wording adds nothing and returns null; a missing argument is an error.

updateNeed.help: Changes the wording of a need.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.needId: The id of the need as read() lists it under vocs[].needs. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new wording. Empty wording changes nothing and returns false; a missing argument is an error.

deleteNeed.help: Removes a need with its drivers and requirements.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.needId: The id of the need. An unknown id is an error.

addDriver.help: Adds a driver under a need.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.needId: The id of the need. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The wording of the driver. Empty wording adds nothing and returns null; a missing argument is an error.
params.type: The driver's type: ctq for quality, ctd for delivery, ctc for cost — what is decisive to the customer about quality, delivery or cost (Critical to Quality, Delivery, Cost). Any other value is an error.

updateDriver.help: Changes the wording and kind of a driver.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.needId: The id of the need. An unknown id is an error.
params.drvId: The id of the driver as read() lists it under vocs[].needs[].drivers. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new wording. Empty wording changes nothing and returns false; a missing argument is an error.
params.type: The driver's type: ctq for quality, ctd for delivery, ctc for cost — what is decisive to the customer about quality, delivery or cost (Critical to Quality, Delivery, Cost). Any other value is an error.

deleteDriver.help: Removes a driver with its requirements.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.needId: The id of the need. An unknown id is an error.
params.drvId: The id of the driver. An unknown id is an error.

addRequirement.help: Adds a requirement under a driver.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.needId: The id of the need. An unknown id is an error.
params.drvId: The id of the driver. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The wording of the requirement. Empty wording adds nothing and returns null; a missing argument is an error.
params.target: The target value the requirement is checked against, e.g. "at most 24 hours". Empty means no target; anything but text is an error.
params.measure: The measure used to check the target value, e.g. "lead time in hours". Empty means no measure; anything but text is an error.

updateRequirement.help: Changes the wording, target value and measure of a requirement.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.needId: The id of the need. An unknown id is an error.
params.drvId: The id of the driver. An unknown id is an error.
params.reqId: The id of the requirement as read() lists it under vocs[].needs[].drivers[].requirements. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new wording. Empty wording changes nothing and returns false; a missing argument is an error.
params.target: The new target value. An empty string clears it; a missing argument is an error.
params.measure: The new measure. An empty string clears it; a missing argument is an error.

params.vocId: The id of the statement. An unknown id is an error.
params.needId: The id of the need. An unknown id is an error.
params.drvId: The id of the driver. An unknown id is an error.
params.reqId: The id of the requirement. An unknown id is an error.

reorderNodes.help: Moves a node to the slot of one of its siblings.

params.kind: The level the move happens on: need, driver or req. Any other value is an error.
params.scope: The parent chain as an object: vocId for a need, plus needId for a driver, plus drvId for a requirement. An unknown id in it is an error.
params.fromId: The id of the node being moved. It must sit on the named level; otherwise it is an error.
params.toId: The id of the sibling whose slot it takes. The same id as fromId leaves the order untouched and returns false; an id outside the sibling list is an error.

setBorderWidth.help: Sets the border width of the nodes.

params.width: The border width in pixels: 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5 or 4. Any other value is an error.

setNodeColor.help: Sets the colour of one node type in the tree.

params.key: Which node type; each is described individually under keys. Any other value is an error.
params.color: The colour; notation and default are given per node type under keys. Any other notation is an error.

vocs.help: The voice-of-customer statements in insertion order. Per statement: id (that is how the actions address it), text, source (where it came from) and needs. Per need: id, text and drivers. Per driver: id, text, type (ctq, ctd or ctc) and requirements. Per requirement: id, text, target (the target value) and measure.

activeVocId.help: The id of the statement whose tree is shown; null means none is selected.

styles.help: The appearance of the tree: borderWidth as the node border width in pixels from 0 to 4 in steps of 0.5, and colors with one colour as rgba(r,g,b,a) under each of voc, need, ctq, ctd, ctc and req.

NodeColors.voc: Colour of the voice-of-customer statements (VoC) in the tree, written as rgb(r,g,b) or rgba(r,g,b,a) with an alpha value from 0 to 1, e.g. rgba(230,126,34,1). The default is a strong orange. Background, border and lines of the nodes are derived from this colour.
NodeColors.need: Colour of the customer needs in the tree, written as rgb(r,g,b) or rgba(r,g,b,a) with an alpha value from 0 to 1, e.g. rgba(155,89,182,1). The default is a violet. Background, border and lines of the nodes are derived from this colour.
NodeColors.ctq: Colour of the drivers of kind CTQ (Critical to Quality) in the tree, written as rgb(r,g,b) or rgba(r,g,b,a) with an alpha value from 0 to 1, e.g. rgba(39,174,96,1). The default is a green. Background, border and lines of the nodes are derived from this colour.
NodeColors.ctd: Colour of the drivers of kind CTD (Critical to Delivery) in the tree, written as rgb(r,g,b) or rgba(r,g,b,a) with an alpha value from 0 to 1, e.g. rgba(41,128,185,1). The default is a blue. Background, border and lines of the nodes are derived from this colour.
NodeColors.ctc: Colour of the drivers of kind CTC (Critical to Cost) in the tree, written as rgb(r,g,b) or rgba(r,g,b,a) with an alpha value from 0 to 1, e.g. rgba(231,76,139,1). The default is a pink. Background, border and lines of the nodes are derived from this colour.
NodeColors.req: Colour of the requirements in the tree, written as rgb(r,g,b) or rgba(r,g,b,a) with an alpha value from 0 to 1, e.g. rgba(94,88,216,1). The default is a blue-violet. Background, border and lines of the nodes are derived from this colour.

kano.name: Kano Model
kano.description: Classify and prioritize requirements from the VoC→CTx tree using the Kano method
kano.sourceNone: No VoC→CTx tree in this project yet. Create one first to pull in requirements.
kano.levelChangeConfirm: Changing the level rebuilds the item list. All captured answers will be lost. Continue?
kano.syncClean: Item list is up to date with the tree.
kano.syncPending: {added} new, {renamed} renamed, {missing} no longer in the tree
kano.syncDetached: Items are not linked to any tree.
kano.sourceDetachedInfo: These items are not linked to any tree. Select a tree above to link them.
kano.respondentDeleteConfirm: Delete this respondent along with all their answers?
kano.captureEmpty: No items yet. Pull in requirements from the tree first.
kano.captureNoRespondent: Add a respondent to start capturing answers.
kano.scale5: I would dislike it a lot
kano.tieTitle: Two categories tied — the stronger category was chosen
kano.warnQShare: High share of questionable answers ({share}) — the questions were likely misunderstood.
kano.whenToUse: When features should be classified by how much their presence raises satisfaction and their absence lowers it — must-be, performance and delight features, surveyed with the functional and the dysfunctional question per respondent; not for weighting criteria against each other, that is what the pairwise comparison is for.

read.help: Returns the capture, the respondents and the selectable trees.

params.options: Optional; this module holds no bulk data.

setSourceTree.help: Links the features to an instance of the VoC-CTx tree module.

params.instanceId: The instance of the tree module the features come from, or null for no link. An instance that does not exist in this project is an error.

setSourceLevel.help: Sets the tree level the features come from. The feature list and all captured answers are discarded, because they belong to the old level.

params.level: The tree level: need for needs, driver for drivers, req for requirements. Any other value is an error.

setImportance.help: Turns the third question about importance on or off.

params.enabled: true captures importance as well and lets it drive the bubble size of the evaluation, false drops the question. Any other value is an error.

applySync.help: Takes over the features of the configured level from the linked tree: new ones are added, renamed ones are updated, ones no longer in the tree are marked as missing. Nothing is ever deleted. Without a link there is nothing to take over, so nothing happens.

setItems.help: Replaces the list of features to be rated.

params.items: The features as an array of objects. Per feature id is required and must be unique; label (its name), path (where it comes from), nodeId (the node in the tree, null for a detached feature) and missing (whether the node is gone) are optional. A missing or duplicate id, an unknown field and a wrong type are errors.

addRespondent.help: Adds a respondent and returns their id. The first respondent is selected in the process.

params.name: The name of the new respondent. Omitted or empty assigns a running default name. A value that is not a string is an error.

params.id: The id of the respondent as read() lists it under respondents. An unknown id is an error.
params.name: The new name. An empty name leaves the old one in place and returns false; a missing argument is an error.

deleteRespondent.help: Removes a respondent with all of their answers. If they were selected, the first remaining one takes over.

params.id: The id of the respondent. An unknown id is an error.

selectRespondent.help: Selects the respondent whose answers the capture grid shows. Answer data stays untouched. A click on the tab is enough; a double click renames the respondent.

params.id: The id of the respondent, or null for no selection. Any other value is an error.

setAnswer.help: Sets a single answer of one respondent for one feature.

params.respondentId: The id of the respondent. An unknown id is an error.
params.itemId: The id of the feature as read() lists it under items. An unknown id is an error.
params.field: Which field; each is described individually under keys. Any other value is an error.
params.value: The value; type and allowed range per field are given under keys.

removeItem.help: Removes a feature with all answers for it.

params.id: The id of the feature. An unknown id is an error.

treeList.help: The VoC-CTx trees of the project the items can be read from — exactly the instanceId values setSourceTree accepts. Per tree: instanceId and name.

source.help: Where the features come from. instanceId names the instance of the VoC-CTx tree module they are read from — the features therefore come from another module instance of the same project; null means detached, the features then stand on their own. level names the level of that tree: need, driver or req.

options.help: The capture options. importance turns the third question about importance on or off; it drives the bubble size of the evaluation.

items.help: The features to be rated, in capture order. Per feature: id (that is how the actions address it), nodeId (the node in the tree, null for a detached feature), label (its name), path (where it comes from in the tree) and missing (whether the node is gone from the tree). Bulk data: without options.fields = ['items'] only the extent is returned.

respondents.help: The respondents in insertion order. Per respondent: id (that is how the actions address them) and name.

answers.help: The answers, by respondent and within that by feature: { respondentId: { itemId: { f, d, w } } }. f is the functional, d the dysfunctional answer on the 1 to 5 scale, w the importance on the 1 to 9 scale; null means unanswered.

activeRespondentId.help: The id of the respondent whose answers the capture grid shows; null means none is selected.

evaluation.help: The evaluation per feature and overall, each entry described individually under keys.

AnswerField.f: The functional question: how would you feel if the feature is present? Five levels: 1 I would be very happy, 2 I expect it, 3 I am indifferent to it, 4 I could accept it, 5 I would dislike it a lot; empty means unanswered. Together with the dysfunctional answer it gives the category of this answer by Kano's evaluation table: happy when present and annoyed when absent is a performance feature; happy when present and neutral when absent is an attractive feature; neutral when present and annoyed when absent is a must-be feature; neutral both ways is indifferent. A pair is questionable only for 1 and 1 or 5 and 5. It is reverse when the absence would make you very happy (1) while the presence is only expected, neutral or acceptable (2 to 4), or when the presence would annoy you a lot (5) but the absence would not (1 to 4); other pairs such as 3 and 2 are indifferent. If either answer is missing, the pair is not classified.
AnswerField.d: The dysfunctional question: how would you feel if the feature is absent? The same five levels as the functional question: 1 I would be very happy, 2 I expect it, 3 I am indifferent to it, 4 I could accept it, 5 I would dislike it a lot; empty means unanswered. Only the pair of functional and dysfunctional answer gives the category by Kano's evaluation table; if either is missing, the pair is not classified.
AnswerField.w: How important the feature is to the respondent, from 1 not at all important to 9 extremely important; empty means unanswered. It is only captured and evaluated when the option "Capture importance" is on; it then sets the order within a category and the bubble size in the chart.

KanoEvaluation.rows: One row of the result table per feature. Sorted by category strength (must-be, performance, attractive, indifferent, reverse, questionable, features without a category last), within a category by mean importance descending, then by CS descending.
KanoEvaluation.totals: The figures across all features and respondents: number of features, number of respondents, completeness and Q share.

KanoRow.itemId: The id of the feature, which the actions use to address it.
KanoRow.label: The name of the feature as the result table shows it.
KanoRow.path: Where the feature sits in the VoC→CTx tree, as a path from top to bottom.
KanoRow.missing: Whether the feature no longer exists in the linked tree. Its answers are kept; the row is marked as missing.
KanoRow.counts: How many respondents put the feature into which category; one number per category.
KanoRow.n: The number of answers for this feature that could be classified, that is a pair of functional and dysfunctional answer. It is the sum of all six categories, including questionable and reverse.
KanoRow.unanswered: The number of answers for this feature that cannot be assigned to any category: because the functional or the dysfunctional answer is missing or because a value lies outside the scale of 1 to 5. They count in no category.
KanoRow.category: The most frequent category among the answers for this feature: must-be, performance, attractive, indifferent, reverse or questionable; empty if no answer could be classified. If two or more categories are equally frequent, the stronger one wins in the order must-be, performance, attractive, indifferent, reverse, questionable.
KanoRow.tie: Whether two or more categories are equally frequent at the top. The stronger one by the category order then applies, and the result table marks the tie.
KanoRow.cs: The satisfaction coefficient (Better): (attractive + performance) divided by (attractive + performance + must-be + indifferent), a value from 0 to 1. Near 1, fulfilling the feature raises satisfaction strongly. Reverse and questionable answers are not in the denominator; empty if no answer falls into these four categories.
KanoRow.ds: The dissatisfaction coefficient (Worse): −(performance + must-be) divided by (attractive + performance + must-be + indifferent), a value from −1 to 0. Near −1, lacking the feature annoys strongly. Reverse and questionable answers are not in the denominator; empty if no answer falls into these four categories.
KanoRow.importanceMean: The mean of the importance ratings from 1 to 9 for this feature. Empty if the option "Capture importance" is off or there is no rating.
KanoRow.importanceN: The number of importance ratings the mean importance is built from; 0 without the option "Capture importance".

KanoCounts.M: Must-be: presence is expected or neutral, absence annoys strongly. The number of respondents who classify the feature this way.
KanoCounts.O: Performance: presence pleases, absence annoys; the better fulfilled, the more satisfied. The number of respondents who classify the feature this way.
KanoCounts.A: Attractive: presence delights, absence is neutral and not missed. The number of respondents who classify the feature this way.
KanoCounts.I: Indifferent: presence and absence are both neutral, the feature hardly affects satisfaction. The number of respondents who classify the feature this way.
KanoCounts.R: Reverse: the answers run against the expected direction, namely when the absence would make you very happy (1) while the presence is only expected, neutral or acceptable (2 to 4), or when the presence would annoy you a lot (5) but the absence would not (1 to 4). The number of respondents who classify the feature this way.
KanoCounts.Q: Questionable: both answers are equally extreme (1 and 1 or 5 and 5) and contradict each other, the question was probably misunderstood. The number of respondents who classify the feature this way.

KanoTotals.items: The number of features being rated.
KanoTotals.completeness: The share of classified answers among all possible ones: classified answers divided by (number of features times number of respondents), a value from 0 to 1; 0 if there are no features or respondents. The interface shows it as a percentage.
KanoTotals.qShare: The share of questionable answers among the classified ones: number of questionable answers divided by number of classified ones, a value from 0 to 1; 0 without classified answers. Above 10 %, the interface warns that the questions were probably misunderstood.

survey-builder.whenToUse: When customers or stakeholders are to be surveyed in writing: design the questionnaire, send it as an HTML file per recipient, read in the answer files and evaluate them — without a server, the data stays in the project.

read.help: Read the questionnaire, recipients, imported responses, hand-overs and the state of the interface.

setTab.help: Open a tab: draft, recipients or results.

setHeader.help: Set a field in the header of the questionnaire: title, introduction, contact, language of the file or anonymous.

params.key: Which header field.
params.value: Text for title, introduction and contact; de or en for the language; true or false for anonymous.

addSection.help: Append an empty section to the end of the questionnaire. Questions always sit in a section.

setSectionField.help: Set the title or the hint of a section.

params.key: Title or hint.
params.value: The new text; empty clears it.

moveSection.help: Move a section one place up or down. Conditions that would then point at a later question are removed; the return value counts them.

deleteSection.help: Delete a section with its questions, without asking. Conditions on these questions are removed; the return value counts them.

addQuestion.help: Append a question of a type to a section and select it.

params.type: single (single choice), multi (multiple choice), rating (rating 1–5), kano (Kano pair), text (free text) or info (text only).

setQuestionField.help: Set the text, the hint or a switch of a question; which switches exist depends on the type.

params.key: Which field.
params.value: Text for text and hint; true or false for the switches.

changeQuestionType.help: Change the type of a question. Text, hint, required and conditions stay, options, rows and switches start empty; conditions on its previous options are removed.

params.type: The new type, values as for addQuestion.

moveQuestion.help: Move a question one place up or down; at a section boundary it moves into the neighbouring section. Conditions that would then point at a later question are removed; the return value counts them.

deleteQuestion.help: Delete a question, without asking — also when imported responses answered it. Conditions on it are removed; the return value counts them.

addItem.help: Append an empty option (single and multiple choice) or row (rating, Kano) to a question.

setItemField.help: Set the text of an option or row, for multiple choice also the display group of an option.

params.key: Text or group.
params.value: The new text; empty clears it.

moveItem.help: Move an option or row one place up or down within its question.

deleteItem.help: Delete an option or row, without asking. Conditions on a deleted option are removed; the return value counts them.

setConditions.help: Decides when a section or question appears: as soon as one of the named options was chosen in an earlier single or multiple choice question. Each condition suffices on its own; without a condition it always appears.

params.conditions: Per condition { questionId, optionIds }: an earlier single or multiple choice question and at least one of its options; [] removes all conditions.

addRecipient.help: Add an empty recipient. Each recipient gets their own questionnaire file, whose answers identify the recipient.

setRecipientField.help: Set a field of a recipient: name, organisation, group, e-mail or note.

params.key: Which field.
params.value: The new text; empty clears it.

deleteRecipient.help: Delete a recipient, without asking. Their responses are kept, without a recipient.

importResponse.help: Read in an answer file the questionnaire saved on the recipient's side. Files of this questionnaire are taken in, also those of an older version; a file read before, one of another questionnaire or a broken one only shows in the log.

params.json: The content of the answer file as text.
params.fileName: The name shown in the log.

deleteResponse.help: Delete an imported response, without asking; its VoC take-over marks go with it.

setFilter.help: Narrow the evaluation to the responses that chose a given option in a single or multiple choice question. Without a filter all responses count.

params.questionId: The choice question; null together with optionId null lifts the filter.
params.optionId: One of its options; null lifts the filter.

setGroupBy.help: Compare the evaluation across the options of a single choice question, for example by customer group. Groups with few responses are marked.

params.questionId: The single choice question; null switches the comparison off.

setReportWithNames.help: Whether the exported report names who wrote the free texts. No effect for an anonymous questionnaire.

params.on: true names them, false does not.

takeToVocTree.help: Take the ticked free texts and other-answers as voices of the customer into the project's VoC tree; if there is none, one is created. Answers taken over before can be taken over again.

params.keys: Answer keys <responseId>:<questionId>, for an other-answer with the suffix :other; the ids are in read().responses.

setKanoTarget.help: Choose which Kano instance of the project a Kano question is handed to, or a new one.

params.instanceId: A Kano instance of the project; null creates a new one at the next hand-over.

handOverToKano.help: Hand a Kano question with all responses, without filter, to the chosen Kano instance or to a new one in this phase. A repeat hand-over replaces only what came from this question.

toWorksheet.help: Create a new worksheet in this phase with all responses, one row per response.

survey.help: The questionnaire: header, version, sections with their questions, options, rows and conditions.

recipients.help: The recipients with name, organisation, group, e-mail and note, plus when and with which version they got their file.

responses.help: The imported responses: per answer file the version, the recipient if known and not anonymous, the time and the answers per question.

answeredRecipientIds.help: Which recipients have answered; this gives the status not sent, sent or answered.

transfers.help: What was handed over: the answers taken into the VoC tree and per Kano question the Kano instance it goes to.

ui.help: State of the interface: open tab, selected question, filter, grouping and whether the report names respondents.

dirtyStructure.help: Whether the structure changed since the last export; once the questionnaire was sent, the next export then raises the version.

exportedOnce.help: Whether the questionnaire was exported at least once.

SurveyHeader.title: The title above the questionnaire.
SurveyHeader.lang: The language of the exported file: German or English.
SurveyHeader.anonymous: Anonymous: answers carry no recipient, even when the file was made for a recipient.

QuestionFields.text: The question as respondents read it.
QuestionFields.required: Required: without an answer the questionnaire cannot be completed.
QuestionFields.noAnswer: Offers a "No answer" choice per row.
QuestionFields.importance: Also asks for the importance from 1 to 9 per row.
QuestionFields.multiline: Multi-line answer field instead of a single line.

ItemFields.text: The text of the option or row.
ItemFields.group: The display group of an option in multiple choice; options of the same group stand together.

RecipientFields.name: Name of the person or company.
RecipientFields.group: The group the response rate is split by.
RecipientFields.email: E-mail address, to send the file with your own mail program.

columns.respondent: Who answered: the recipient, anonymous or without recipient.
columns.sentAt: When the file for the recipient was made and with which version of the questionnaire.
columns.sent: How many recipients got their file.
columns.rate: Response rate: answered divided by sent.
columns.n: How many responses count for the row.
columns.dist: How often each level from 1 to 5 was chosen.
columns.na: How often no answer was chosen.
columns.category: The Kano category of the row, determined from the answer pairs.
columns.better: Satisfaction coefficient: how much the feature delights when present, from 0 to 1.
columns.worse: Dissatisfaction coefficient: how much its absence annoys; the larger the magnitude, the stronger.
columns.share: Its share of the responses to the question.

runner.noscript: This questionnaire needs JavaScript. Please open the file in a current browser.
runner.kanoImportance: How important is it to you?
runner.resetConfirm: Delete all answers and start over?
runner.draftOutdated: This questionnaire has changed since you started filling it in. Your previous answers have been kept – please check them.
runner.saved: The file “{file}” has been saved. Please send it back to the contact person.

process-map.name: Process Map
process-map.description: Visual process flow with inputs and outputs per step
process-map.whenToUse: When an existing process needs documenting as a horizontal step chain with inputs, outputs, value-add classification and rework loops — not for a pure role or decision view, that is Deployment resp. Activity Flowchart.

addStep.help: Inserts a new, empty step at a gap in the chain; the agent gets the identifier of the new step back.

params.atIndex: The gap to insert at (0 = before the first step, up to the chain length = at the end). A value outside that range or a non-integer is an error.

removeStep.help: Removes a step from the chain. Any loop targeting it is removed too.

params.id: The id of the step to remove. An unknown id is an error.

addIO.help: Appends an input or output to a step; the agent gets the identifier of the new entry back.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.type: 'inputs' or 'outputs'. Any other value is an error.

removeIO.help: Removes an input or output from a step.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.type: 'inputs' or 'outputs'. Any other value is an error.
params.ioId: The entry's id. An unknown id is an error.

cycleInputType.help: Cycles an input's type: none → process parameter (x) → noise factor (n) → none.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.ioId: The input's id. An unknown id is an error.

cycleValueType.help: Cycles a step's value type: unclassified → value-adding (VA) → business non-value-adding (BNVA) → non-value-adding (NVA) → unclassified.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new title.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new description.

setIOName.help: Sets the name of an input or output.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.type: 'inputs' or 'outputs'. Any other value is an error.
params.ioId: The entry's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.name: The new name.

setLoop.help: Creates or removes a step's loop. A newly created loop is empty — no condition, target or rework steps; removing one takes those details with it.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.on: true creates the loop, false removes it.

setLoopCondition.help: Sets a loop's trigger condition. If the step carries no loop, nothing happens.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new condition.

setLoopTarget.help: Sets a loop's target step (which earlier step it loops back to). Without a target step the loop's target is cleared. If the step carries no loop, or the chosen target step does not come before this step in the chain, nothing happens.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.targetStepId: The id of an existing step. Leave empty (or null) to clear the loop's target. An unknown id is an error; a known id that does not lie before the step with the loop changes nothing (returns false).

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.

addLoopStep.help: Appends a rework step to a step's loop and returns its id. Returns null if the step carries no loop — nothing happens then.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.

removeLoopStep.help: Removes a rework step from a step's loop.

params.stepId: The step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.loopStepId: The rework step's id. An unknown id is an error.

params.stepId: The id of the step carrying the loop. An unknown id is an error.
params.loopStepId: The rework step's id. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new title.

setSubstepsExpanded.help: Shows or hides a step's sub-steps; display only, the content stays.

params.stepId: The id of the step whose sub-steps are shown or hidden. An unknown id is an error.
params.expanded: true shows the sub-steps, false hides them.

addSubstep.help: Adds an empty sub-step to a step.

params.stepId: The id of the step that gets the new sub-step. An unknown id is an error.

removeSubstep.help: Removes a sub-step from its parent step.

params.parentId: The id of the parent step. An unknown id is an error.
params.substepId: The id of the sub-step to remove.

params.stepId: The id of the parent step. An unknown id is an error.
params.substepId: The id of the sub-step. An unknown id is an error.
params.text: The new title.

process-map.insertHere: Insert here — or drop a card here to move it
process-map.importFromSipocHint: Pick a SIPOC. Every entry in its P column will be appended as a process step.

steps.help: The chain in order. Each step carries id, title, description, valueType (null|'va'|'bnva'|'nva'), inputs and outputs (each with id, name, optionally inputType 'param'|'noise' on inputs), substeps (each with id, title), expanded and loop (null, or { condition, targetStepId, steps: [{id,title}] }).

raci-matrix.name: RACI Matrix
raci-matrix.description: Responsibility Assignment Matrix: roles per activity and stakeholder
raci-matrix.whenToUse: When each activity of an undertaking needs a record of who does the work (R), who is accountable (A), who is consulted (C) and who is informed (I) — the check reports every row without an R, without an A or with more than one A; not for describing the flow itself, which is what a flowchart is for.

addActivity.help: Appends an activity (row) with the entered name to the matrix; its row number, counted from 0, comes back as the answer.

params.text: The name of the activity; surrounding whitespace is dropped. An empty text adds nothing and returns -1 — that is a refusal, not an error.

addStakeholder.help: Appends a stakeholder (column) with the entered name to the matrix; its column number, counted from 0, comes back as the answer.

params.text: The name of the stakeholder; surrounding whitespace is dropped. An empty text adds nothing and returns -1 — that is a refusal, not an error.

setRole.help: Sets the role of a cell absolutely.

params.aIdx: The row number of the activity, counted from 0. A number that names no activity is an error.
params.sIdx: The column number of the stakeholder, counted from 0. A number that names no stakeholder is an error.
params.role: The role: R (responsible, does the work), A (accountable), C (consulted) or I (informed). The empty text takes the role back. Any other value is an error.

cycleRole.help: Advances the role of a cell by one step, like a click on the cell: no role to R, R to A, A to C, C to I, I back to no role. R means does the work, A is accountable, C is consulted, I is informed. A specific value can also be set directly.

params.aIdx: The row number of the activity, counted from 0. A number that names no activity is an error.
params.sIdx: The column number of the stakeholder, counted from 0. A number that names no stakeholder is an error.

params.idx: The row number of the activity, counted from 0. A number that names no activity is an error.
params.value: The new name. An empty text is rejected and leaves the old name in place (returns false).

params.idx: The column number of the stakeholder, counted from 0. A number that names no stakeholder is an error.
params.value: The new name. An empty text is rejected and leaves the old name in place (returns false).

removeActivity.help: Removes an activity together with its roles; the remaining rows move up.

params.idx: The row number of the activity, counted from 0. A number that names no activity is an error.

removeStakeholder.help: Removes a stakeholder together with its roles; the remaining columns move left.

params.idx: The column number of the stakeholder, counted from 0. A number that names no stakeholder is an error.

moveActivity.help: Moves an activity to another place in the order; its roles travel along.

params.from: The row number of the activity, counted from 0. A number that names no activity is an error.
